the-mad-podcast-with-matt-turck.name: The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
the-mad-podcast-with-matt-turck.bio: Podcast: When AI Improves Itself | Richard Socher (Recursive)

html_en:
The mood in AI circles today is unmistakably optimistic — about building, about science, about what comes next — even as the first tremors of the agentic era raise genuinely unsettling questions about who, or what, is in control.

🔬 The Recursive Dream: AI That Fixes Science's Slow Burn

The most substantive conversation of the day comes from the MAD Podcast, where Matt Turck sits down with Richard Socher — one of AI's most-cited researchers — fresh off raising $650 million for his company Recursive. The subject: recursive self-improvement, and the audacious claim that AI might rescue science from itself.

Watch/Listen: When AI Improves Itself | Richard Socher (The MAD Podcast)

Socher's book, The Eureka Machine, opens with a counterintuitive premise — that scientific progress has quietly stalled. His argument is structural, not defeatist.

"We evolved from a body of knowledge to a labyrinth of knowledge — 34,000 journals that might as well have no trespassing signs." — Richard Socher

The Renaissance polymath, he argues, could synthesize across disciplines precisely because the total body of human knowledge was small enough to hold in one head. Today, even a PhD biologist is lost the moment a conversation drifts from their precise sub-layer of the field. The result: fewer cross-disciplinary sparks, fewer E=MC² moments, more incremental engineering.

"What AI is, calculus did for physics — AI will do for biology. It'll help us weave back together lots of very complex pieces that build these complex systems." — Richard Socher

And the recursive self-improvement angle? Socher's bet is that simulated environments will do for AI what wind tunnels did for aeronautics.

"Anything you can simulate, AI will solve. And before you know it, you're in this recursive self-improvement loop... Boy, are we far away from the true upper bounds of any of the spaces of intelligence." — Richard Socher

Six hundred and fifty million dollars says someone believes him.

🤖 The Agent Economy: Everyone Wants a Piece of Your Workflow

The week's chatter about personal AI agents — tools like Muse that handle tasks end-to-end on your behalf — crystallized nicely in a sharp post from Box CEO Aaron Levie, who called the shift the biggest consumer tech disruption since the App Store.

"The new attention you need to compete for is not from the user itself but instead for the agent. This means that the tools that allow agents to order food, handle ecommerce transactions, book flights, work with the local economy, and interact with our data and information best, are the ones that will get used the most." — @levie

It's an elegant reframe: in the agentic era, your product's real customer may be a bot, not a human. The implications for UX, APIs, and MCP tooling are enormous — and largely unresolved.

On the ground, the rollout remains bumpy. @thenanyu reported that both Muse and Instinct claim to be unable to place calls — a reminder that the vision and the product are still some distance apart.

Meanwhile, Peter Yang offered a charming, small-scale proof of concept: a personal Markdown file paired with a /tastemaker skill that tracks his movie and book ratings, then surfaces eerily relevant new suggestions each week. He's floating the idea of open-sourcing it — the kind of quiet, practical agent use case that often spreads faster than the splashy enterprise demos.

🛠️ Learn by Doing: The Builder Ethos Takes Hold

Two of the day's most-liked posts converge on the same idea: in a fast-moving field, tinkering is the only reliable epistemology.

Guillermo Rauch, Vercel's CEO, put it warmly and broadly:

"The coolest thing about the recent wave of AI is that everyone is excited about building. All short-term drama aside, this is an immeasurably good development for the world. The people want to create and ship, not just consume." — @rauchg

Nikunj Kothari, a VC who codes for two hours every day, made the same case from an investor's angle — with a methodical breakdown of why hands-on practice is non-negotiable right now:

"Unlike other eras, things are moving SO fast that if you don't do this, I simply don't understand how folks will ever learn what's coming next... You have to understand the model capabilities to see where the next set of models will improve — still so much alpha in reading technical papers." — @nikunj

His three-part framework — model capabilities, infrastructure needs, application-layer harnesses — is a tidy map of where the real bets are being made. The meta-point is harder to argue with: you cannot invest intelligently in something you've never touched.

⚠️ The Security Undercurrent Nobody Wants to Talk About

Amid all the optimism, @adityaag dropped a note that deserves more attention than it got:

"After seeing the rush of announcements by Gemini, OpenAI and Anthropic about even more agent intrusions... I take it for 100% granted that a number of major companies have been penetrated by nation states without them knowing about it." — @adityaag

It's speculative, but not paranoid. As agents gain persistent access to enterprise tools, calendars, codebases, and financial accounts, the attack surface expands in ways that traditional security models weren't designed to handle. The industry is moving fast; the adversaries are moving faster. This is the conversation that will matter more with every capability announcement — and it's still mostly happening in the margins.
html_zh:
AI 自我改进的浪潮正在悄然重塑科学研究的边界，与此同时，个人智能体的崛起正将整个消费科技格局带入一场自 App Store 以来最大的变革。

🔬 科学的迷宫与 AI 的钥匙：Richard Socher 的"递归"雄心

本周最值得细读的一段对话，来自 The MAD Podcast，主持人 Matt Turck 与 AI 领域引用率最高的研究者之一、刚刚为其新公司 Recursive 融资 6.5 亿美元的 Richard Socher 深度对谈。Socher 即将出版新书 The Eureka Machine，核心命题令人警醒：人类科学进步正在放缓。

"我们已经从一个知识体，演变成了一座知识迷宫——三万四千种学术期刊，每一扇门上都像贴着'禁止入内'的告示。"——Matt Turck 转述 Socher 书中观点

Socher 的诊断犀利：现代科学被切割成无数细分领域，每个领域都需要数年才能深入，跨学科的"文艺复兴式天才"已近乎绝迹。抗生素彻底攻克了细菌感染，但癌症与病毒至今悬而未决；爱因斯坦级别的物理突破，几十年来杳无音讯。

"AI 将对生物学做到微积分对物理学所做的事——它将帮助我们把无数复杂碎片重新编织在一起，理解大脑为何能产生思想，微生物组为何能影响整个身体。"——Richard Socher

而他的答案，就是"递归自我改进"（RSI）：让 AI 不断优化自身，在模拟环境中迭代突破。Watch/Listen: When AI Improves Itself | Richard Socher (Recursive) — The MAD Podcast

🤖 个人智能体：下一个 App Store 时刻

如果说 Socher 描绘的是 AI 的科研未来，那么 Box 创始人 Aaron Levie 这周则点出了 AI 最近期、最具爆发力的商业机会：个人智能体（Personal Agents）。

"个人智能体是'为智能体构建产品'这一理念的终极体现。你想要的形态是：把一项任务交给智能体，确保它能端到端完整完成。为此，智能体必须能够操作你的工具，或者使用自己的工具——调用 MCP、访问 CLI、在你的网站上顺畅导航、完成交易……新的注意力争夺，不再来自用户本身，而是来自智能体。"——@levie

Levie 将此定性为"自 App Store 以来消费科技领域最大的机会与洗牌"。能让智能体订餐、订机票、处理电商交易、与本地经济无缝对接的工具，将成为新时代的基础设施。与此同时，也有用户已经遭遇现实摩擦——@thenanyu 反映，尝试使用 Muse 和 Instinct 拨打电话时，两款产品均表示功能尚未就绪，提示这一愿景的落地仍在进行中。

💡 VC 下场写代码，投资人如何跟上 AI 速度

当 AI 以如此速度演进，如何保持真正的判断力？投资人 @nikunj 给出了他自己的答案：每天亲自动手写两小时代码。

"事情移动得如此之快，如果你不这样做，我真不明白人们怎么能理解下一步会发生什么。读技术论文依然有巨大的 alpha；你需要亲眼看到模型需要什么工具才能完成更长链条的任务；你需要理解让模型帮助构建自主公司的'框架能力'。你显然也可以靠和研究者、创始人交流来学习——但我从来不是那种不动手就能学会东西的人。"——@nikunj

这与 Vercel CEO @rauchg 的观察形成共鸣：

"这一波 AI 浪潮最酷的地方在于，所有人都对'构建'感到兴奋。抛开所有短期的喧嚣，这对世界而言是一件无比美好的事。人们想要创造、想要交付，而不仅仅是消费。"——@rauchg

💰 ChatGPT 帮你管钱，AI 理财提示即将到来

更接地气的应用场景这周也有预告。前产品人、播客主 @petergyang 宣布即将发布一集关于 ChatGPT 个人理财的播客，对话嘉宾是 OpenAI ChatGPT Finances 产品负责人 @ebloch，内容涵盖六个实用提示词，涉及主动寻找税务节省、最大化信用卡奖励、创建财务独立路径预测等场景。

与此同时，Yang 本人也在测试一套更个人化的 AI 工作流：用一个 Markdown 文件追踪自己对电影、剧集、书籍的评分，每周让 AI 据此推荐新内容。他在推文中询问是否应该开源这套工具——目前看来，呼声不小。

🔒 智能体扩张背后的安全暗流

在所有关于智能体扩张的乐观叙事之外，也有人选择泼一盆冷水。安全研究者 @adityaag 写道：

"看到 Gemini、OpenAI 和 Anthropic 接连宣布更多智能体渗透……我几乎可以百分之百确定，已经有多家大公司在不知情的情况下，被国家级行为者入侵了。"——@adityaag

这一警告虽属推测，却并非无稽之谈。当智能体被赋予越来越深的系统权限、越来越长的任务链条，攻击面随之扩大是必然的结果。在为智能体构建"开放的门"的同时，业界对于"谁能走进这扇门"的问题，或许还远未做好准备。
